paragraphs: The situation of the common people is quite different. They have little time to spare for education. Their parents can scarcely afford to support them, even in infancy. As soon as the children are able to work, they must take up some trade in order to earn their living. Such a trade is usually so simple and uniform that it gives the mind very little exercise. Meanwhile, their labour is so constant and so demanding that it leaves them little leisure, and still less inclination, to devote themselves to anything else, or even to think about it.

In no civilized society can the common people be as well instructed as those of some rank and fortune. Nevertheless, the most essential parts of education, namely reading, writing and arithmetic, can be acquired very early in life. As a result, most people, even those destined for the lowest occupations, have time to learn them before they are old enough to be employed. At a very small expense, the public can make it easier for almost the whole population to acquire these essentials. It can encourage people to do so, and it can even impose this necessity upon them.

The public can make this easier by establishing a little school in every parish or district, where children may be taught for a fee so moderate that even a common labourer can afford it. The schoolmaster should be paid partly, but not wholly, by the public. A master paid entirely, or even mainly, from public funds would soon learn to neglect his business. In Scotland, parish schools of this kind have taught almost all the common people to read. A very large proportion of them have also learned to write and keep accounts. In England, charity schools have had a similar effect, though less universally, because they are less widespread. The reading books used in these schools could be somewhat more instructive than they generally are. Moreover, poor children are sometimes given a little smattering of Latin, which is scarcely ever of any use to them. If they learned the elementary parts of geometry and mechanics instead, the education of this class of people would perhaps be as complete as it could be. Almost every common trade offers some opportunity to apply the principles of geometry and mechanics. In this way, the work itself would gradually exercise and improve ordinary people in them. These principles, Smith observes, are the necessary introduction to the most sublime as well as the most useful sciences.
The public can encourage people to acquire these essential skills by awarding small premiums and little badges of distinction to the children of the common people who excel in them.

Lastly, the public can impose this basic education on almost the whole population. It can require every man to pass an examination or probation in these subjects before he can obtain the freedom of a corporation, that is, membership of a trade guild. Without it, he should not be allowed to set up any trade, whether in a village or in a corporate town.
